Actions performed within the three guṇas result in material outcomes and bondage, as these modes are part of Māyā. Even attaining svarga (heaven) through sattvika actions is still a material attainment and does not lead to liberation. When the sattva mode predominates, the person is calm and serene. When the rajas mode prevails, the person becomes active, hopeful, and ambitious for power, passion, and profit. answer.answer:
The Advaitic view, as discussed, faces logical difficulties regarding the nature of ignorance (avidyā). If ignorance is eternal, it implies two eternal entities—Brahman and ignorance—contradicting Advaita's claim of only one entity, Brahman. If ignorance had a beginning and will end, it suggests the soul was once perfect Brahman but was overpowered by ignorance, which undermines the purpose of spiritual practice since ignorance could overpower Brahman again. If ignorance never began but will be destroyed one day, it contradicts the Vedic declaration of eternal creation. Therefore, these views are problematic for Advaita.

The only universally acceptable philosophy is that the individual soul has been overpowered by ignorance due to Māyā since beginningless time, but this ignorance will not stay forever and can be terminated through devotion. However, Māyā itself is eternal and cannot be destroyed. Thus, ignorance is beginningless but not eternal in the sense of being indestructible; it can end for the individual soul, though Māyā as a power remains eternal [1][2].

Aur bhi kai karan ho sakte hain, jaise ki jeevon ko roop aur gunon ke saath Bhagwan ka divya roop dikhana, jisse unka man Bhagwan mein lag sake [4]. Is prakar, Bhagwan ke avatar hone ke peeche mukhya uddeshya jeevon ki mukti, unka kalyan, aur unhe divya prem se paripurn karna hai.

answer.answer: Worldly influences such as desires, anger, greed, and māyā dominate the lives of ordinary beings, causing endless suffering and bondage to the cycle of birth and death. However, those who have realized God perform divine actions (divya karmas) that are beyond the three gunas (qualities) and are not bound by these worldly influences. Such divine actions do not produce the usual results of suffering and bondage. The realized ones are free from attachment and the effects of karma because their actions are done for the sake of God and spiritual aspirants, not for personal gain or worldly desires. Thus, worldly influences cannot affect those who have realized God because their actions transcend the material modes and are aligned with divine will, leading to liberation from the cycle of birth and death [1][3][4].
